Believers
bē-lēv´ẽrz
n. pl. (those who believe; the ordinary New Testament name for the members of the church)
From Old English gelyfan, to believe, to hold dear. The plural noun renders the Greek participle hoi pisteuontes, “the believing ones,” and the adjective pistos used substantively.

Biblical Definition

Believers is one of the plainest names Scripture gives the church, and it is a name of the whole company, not of an inner circle. Luke records the growth of the Jerusalem church in exactly this word: “And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women” (Act 5:14). Two things are asserted there. First, they were added to the Lord — the joining is to a Person before it is to a society. Second, they were believers, which is to say the mark of membership was faith, not birth, not nationality, not ceremony. Paul charges Timothy to “be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity” (1Ti 4:12), and the six terms show what a believer's life is expected to look like from the outside. The same company appears in its common life: “the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul” (Act 4:32), and “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44). Believers in the New Testament are never solitary. The word is plural because faith gathers, and the gathering is visible: a body of men and women, known to each other, added to the Lord and therefore added to one another.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a believer as one who believes; one who gives credit to other evidence than that of personal knowledge; and in theology, one who gives credit to the truth of the Scriptures as a revelation from God.

expand to see more

BELIEV'ER, n. One who believes; one who gives credit to other evidence than that of personal knowledge.

2. In theology, one who gives credit to the truth of the Scriptures, as a revelation from God.

3. In a more restricted sense, a professor of Christianity; one who receives the gospel, as unfolding the true way of salvation, and Christ as his Savior.

BELIEV'ERS, the plural; in the Scriptures, the whole company of those added to the Lord.

Key Scripture

Acts 5:14 — "And believers were the more added to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women."

1 Timothy 4:12 — "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity."

Acts 4:32 — "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common."

Acts 2:44 — "And all that believed were together, and had all things common;"

Modern Corruption

Belief is privatized, so that a believer is understood as an individual holding an opinion rather than a member added to the Lord and to a visible body.

expand to see more

The New Testament has no category for a believer who belongs to no congregation. Luke does not say that believers increased and then, separately, that a church formed; he says believers were added to the Lord, and the immediate consequence in Acts is a body of one heart and one soul with its goods held loosely. The modern habit of treating faith as a private conviction, with church attendance as an optional expression of it, reverses the order of the text. Faith in Christ joins a man to Christ, and no one is joined to the Head without being joined to the members.

The second loss is the visibility of the mark. Paul tells Timothy to be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity — six things others can observe. A believer in Scripture is identifiable: he confesses, he gathers, he gives, he lives differently. Where belief becomes an inward disposition with no required outward shape, the word ceases to name anything, and a church roll fills with names that Acts would not have counted. This is not a plea for perfectionism; it is the plain expectation that what a man believes will show.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pisteuo (G4100), to believe, trust; its participle hoi pisteuontes, the believing ones; pistos (G4103), faithful, believing, used as a noun for the church's members.

expand to see more

Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, entrust oneself to; over two hundred and forty times in the New Testament.

Greek pistos (G4103) — faithful, believing; used substantively of church members in 1 Timothy 4:12 and Acts 10:45.

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, the thing believed and the believing; Hebrews 11:1.

Acts 5:14 says believers were added to the Lord — the union is with Christ first, and with the body because of Him.

The plural is the New Testament's ordinary form; the singular believer standing alone is nearly unknown in Acts.

Usage

"“Believers were the more added to the Lord” — added to Him, and so to one another."

"“Be thou an example of the believers” — in six things others can see."

"“All that believed were together” — Acts knows no solitary Christian."
